newsitem.title: MACEDONIA: EU observers say Macedonian vote flawed.
newsitem.headline: EU observers say Macedonian vote flawed.

text.p: European observers monitoring Macedonia's local elections said on Monday 25 percent of voters could not cast their ballots because they were not on electoral lists.
Macedonians voted in 124 municipalities across the country on Sunday in a poll analysts said would shape the future of the country's national politics.
Early returns indicated opposition parties performed better than expected, although some 90 percent of councils appeared certain to need a second round of voting to decide the eventual outcome.
In a news conference, the 12-member Council of Europe delegation said it visited 96 polling stations and founded registration problems in almost every case.
The problem particularly affected northwest Macedonia, dominated by ethnic Albanians who are at odds with local Macedonians.
The council refused to pass judgment on the fairness of the poll, and limited its comments to direct observations.

One council of Europe delegate Diago Scaceli who visited the northwest said: "There was a lot of irritation and frustration around the polling stations, because in certain cases a mojority of families could not find their names and couldn't vote."
The chairman of the Federal Electoral Commission, Ljiljana Ristova, blamed unsuccessful voters for not checking electoral lists beforehand.
The Europeans' comments appeared to confirm earlier reports of widespread problems which the opposition VMRO - DPME described as "organised chaos".
But Ristova insisted there were no serious problems.
"Our evaluation is that the election was good and in order, and there were no problems of a technical or organisational nature. It was held in a normal way," she told a news conference.
Opposition politicians and analysts said the outcome of the local election would play a role in determining political strategy in national politics.

"This is being seen as a mid-term referendum on the government's performance," said one Western official who declined to be named. "If the opposition parties do well, they'll use that electoral support as a lever to try to push their policies through federal parliament."
Although official results were not expected until late on Tuesday, early unofficial returns indicated that the opposition coalition, led by VMRO - DPME was doing better than expected.
They had seized at least four councils in key electorates and were leading the ruling Social Democrat candidates in regions expected to back the government. The Social Democrats had six councils.
The conservative VMRO campaigned for a new direction for economic reform, describing the Social Democrats' drive for privatisation and a Western-leaning economy as "unjust".

In the crucial Albanian-dominated district, the nationalist Party for Democratic Prosperity of Albanians (PDP-A) appeared to be leading its pro-government rivals, the Party for Democratic Prosperity (PDP).

The PDP-A leader Arben Djaferi told Reuters a good result would indicate his party's aggressive political fight for ethnic rights, including recognition of the Albanian language, and legalisation of the underground University of Tetovo which teaches in Albanian.
